samf-senior-2000-r2-01.title: Approximate the square roots
samf-senior-2000-r2-01.body:
$\sqrt{24}\approx\sqrt{25}=5$ (in fact $4{,}9$), so $\sqrt{24}-1\approx4$ (in fact $3{,}9$), its square root is about $2$ (in fact $1{,}97$) and the fraction is about $\frac32=1{,}5$ (in fact $1{,}52$).

**Answer: (A) 1,5**

samf-senior-2000-r2-05.title: Space diagonal
samf-senior-2000-r2-05.body:
The space diagonal of the cube is the diameter of the sphere. For side $s$ the space diagonal is $s\sqrt3$ (Pythagoras twice: $d^2=2s^2$, $d^2+s^2=3s^2$). So $s\sqrt3=9\sqrt3$, $s=9$ and the volume is $9^3=729$.

**Answer: (B) 729**

samf-senior-2000-r2-06.title: Match numerators
samf-senior-2000-r2-06.body:
Over the common denominator, $A(x+1)+B(x-1)=(A+B)x+(A-B)=3x-5$ for all $x$. So $A+B=3$, $A-B=-5$, giving $A=-1$, $B=4$ and $A^2+B^2=1+16=17$.

**Answer: (B) 17**

samf-senior-2000-r2-07.title: Pythagoras in triangle DCE
samf-senior-2000-r2-07.body:
$DE=DA=\sqrt2$ (radii) and $DC=AB=1$. In the right-angled triangle $DCE$, $CE^2=DE^2-DC^2=2-1=1$, so $CE=1$.

**Answer: (E) 1**

samf-senior-2000-r2-08.title: Find the period
samf-senior-2000-r2-08.body:
The sequence repeats in blocks of nine letters $ABCDEDCBA$. Since $2000=9\cdot222+2$, the 2000th letter is the 2nd letter of a block, which is $B$.

**Answer: (B)**

samf-senior-2000-r2-09.title: Parity
samf-senior-2000-r2-09.body:
A prime $p$ that is a sum of two primes is larger than 2 and so odd. An odd sum of two primes needs one even prime, i.e. the prime 2, and the other is $p-2$. So there is at most one way for each prime. Hence no prime can be written in two different ways.

**Answer: (A) 0**

samf-senior-2000-r2-10.title: Angle sum
samf-senior-2000-r2-10.body:
The interior angles of a hexagon sum to $720^\circ$. Suppose $m$ angles are acute (less than $90^\circ$); the other $6-m$ angles are each less than $180^\circ$ (convex). Then $720<90m+180(6-m)=1080-90m$, so $m<4$ and $m\le3$. Three acute angles are possible: e.g. take a hexagon cut from a long thin triangle-like shape with three angles of $80^\circ$ and three of $160^\circ$ ($3\cdot80+3\cdot160=720$).

**Answer: (B) 3**

samf-senior-2000-r2-11.title: Clear denominators
samf-senior-2000-r2-11.body:
Since $n+16>0$: $5(n+16)<9n$ gives $80<4n$, i.e. $n>20$; and $7n<4(n+16)$ gives $3n<64$, i.e. $n<21\frac13$. So $20<n<21\frac13$ and only $n=21$ works.

**Answer: (D) 1**

samf-senior-2000-r2-12.title: Check residues
samf-senior-2000-r2-12.body:
Only $n \bmod 7$ matters: $0,1,2,3,4,5,6$ give squares with remainders $0,1,4,2,2,4,1$. The distinct remainders are $0,1,2,4$, so there are 4.

**Answer: (C) 4**

samf-senior-2000-r2-13.title: Remainder theorem
samf-senior-2000-r2-13.body:
The remainder on division by $(x-1)(x-2)$ has the form $ax+b$, so $P(x)=(x-1)(x-2)q(x)+ax+b$. Then $P(1)=a+b=2$ and $P(2)=2a+b=1$, giving $a=-1$, $b=3$. The remainder is $-x+3$.

**Answer: (E)**

samf-senior-2000-r2-14.title: Set up an equation
samf-senior-2000-r2-14.body:
With $s$ sheep and $c$ chickens, $\ell=\frac{4s+2c}{s+c}$. So $\ell s+\ell c=4s+2c$, i.e. $(4-\ell)s=(\ell-2)c$ and $\frac sc=\frac{\ell-2}{4-\ell}$.

**Answer: (B)**

samf-senior-2000-r2-14.title: Check with a value
samf-senior-2000-r2-14.body:
If $\ell=3$ the animals are half sheep and half chickens, ratio $1$; (B) gives $\frac{1}{1}=1$, while (A) gives $1$ too but (A) at $\ell=2$ gives $\frac{2}{6}\ne0$ (all chickens means ratio $0$) and (B) gives $0$. Only (B) fits both checks.

**Answer: (B)**

samf-senior-2000-r2-15.title: Count digits
samf-senior-2000-r2-15.body:
Pages 1-9 use 1 digit each (9 digits), pages 10-99 use 2 each, pages 100-999 use 3 each. A book of $k$ pages with $10\le k\le 99$ needs $9+2(k-9)=2k-9$ digits, an odd number up to $189$. A book with $100\le k\le999$ pages needs $189+3(k-99)$ digits: $189$ plus a multiple of 3, i.e. a multiple of 3 between $192$ and $2886$.

31 is odd and less than 189 (so $k=20$). 543, 1998 and 2001 are multiples of 3. But 1999 is not a multiple of 3 and exceeds 189, so it is impossible.

**Answer: (D) 1999**

samf-senior-2000-r2-16.title: Isosceles triangles
samf-senior-2000-r2-16.body:
Join $AE$ and $ED$. Since $DE=DC$ (radii of the second circle), $\angle CED=\theta$. The exterior angle gives $\angle EDA=2\theta$. Since $EA=ED$ (radii of the first circle), $\angle DAE=2\theta$. Since $EA=EB$, $\angle EAB=63^\circ$. Then $\angle BAC=63^\circ+2\theta$ and the angles of triangle $ABC$ give $63^\circ+(63^\circ+2\theta)+\theta=180^\circ$, so $3\theta=54^\circ$ and $\theta=18^\circ$.

**Answer: (A) $18^\circ$**

samf-senior-2000-r2-17.title: Midpoint theorem
samf-senior-2000-r2-17.body:
Since $B$ is fixed and $BC$ has fixed length, $C$ moves on a circle about $B$. The diagonals bisect each other, so the intersection $M$ is the midpoint of $AC$. If $O$ is the midpoint of $AB$ (fixed), then $OM\parallel BC$ and $OM=\frac12BC$. So $M$ stays at a fixed distance $\frac12BC$ from the fixed point $O$: it moves on a circle (or part of one).

**Answer: (A) circle**

samf-senior-2000-r2-18.title: Factor
samf-senior-2000-r2-18.body:
$\frac1m+\frac1n=\frac1{15}$ gives $15(m+n)=mn$, i.e. $(m-15)(n-15)=225$. Since $m,n>15$ (each of $\frac1m,\frac1n<\frac1{15}$), both factors are positive. $225=3^2\cdot5^2$ has $3\cdot3=9$ divisors, each giving exactly one ordered pair.

**Answer: (E) 9**

samf-senior-2000-r2-19.title: Venn diagram
samf-senior-2000-r2-19.body:
Let $x$ be the number speaking only English. All three: 5. Sotho and English only: $9-5=4$. Sotho and Afrikaans only: $12-5=7$. Only Sotho: 0. English and Afrikaans only: $18-5-4-x=9-x$. Afrikaans only: $20-7-5-(9-x)=x-1$. Everyone speaks at least one language (30 people), so
$$0+7+4+5+(x-1)+(9-x)+x=24+x=30,$$
and $x=6$.

**Answer: (B) 6**

samf-senior-2000-r2-20.title: Split on u
samf-senior-2000-r2-20.body:
If $u=0$: $v+w+x+y+z=3$ has $\binom{3+4}{4}=35$ solutions (stars and bars). If $u=1$: $v+w+x+y+z=1$ has $5$ solutions. $u\ge2$ is impossible. Total $35+5=40$.

**Answer: (D) 40**

samf-senior-2000-r2-20.title: Count by type
samf-senior-2000-r2-20.body:
For $u=0$: one variable equal to 3 (5 ways); one equal to 2 and another to 1 ($5\cdot4=20$ ways); three variables equal to 1 ($\binom53=10$ ways): 35. For $u=1$: 5 ways. Total 40.

**Answer: (D)**
